claims.text: A minor boron addition to a marginally glass-forming multicomponent metallic alloy will enhance its glass-forming ability.
Boron is a small-atom element relative to the principal constituents of the proposed Zr-based alloy.
Minor boron addition increases atomic-size mismatch in the alloy.
Increased atomic-size mismatch introduces packing frustration.
Packing frustration kinetically suppresses crystallization and thereby improves glass formation.
The initial Zr-based alloy is crystalline or only marginally glass-forming.
Under standard cooling rates, the initial alloy tends to form coarse crystalline phases.
The proposed intervention is addition of a few atomic percent boron to the base alloy.
Rapid cooling by methods such as melt spinning or suction casting allows differences in critical cooling rate to be evaluated.
Small boron atoms disrupt regular lattice arrangements and increase local topological disorder.
Boron-induced packing frustration lowers atomic mobility.
Lower atomic mobility disrupts nucleation and growth of crystalline phases during cooling.
Suppression of crystal nucleation and growth favors formation of an amorphous structure.
The boron-modified alloy will have an increased critical cooling rate relative to the base alloy.
The boron-modified alloy will require a lower cooling rate to form glass than the base alloy.
Boron addition will produce a larger glass-forming composition window and/or permit thicker amorphous samples.
The unmodified alloy has limited glass-forming ability and tends to crystallize during conventional cooling.
The beneficial effect of boron exists only up to an optimum concentration.
Excess boron may cause boride phases to form.
Very low boron additions may be insufficient to alter alloy packing dynamics.

contradictions.description: Enhanced glass-forming ability is associated with requiring a lower cooling rate, but the predicted outcome also says that boron increases the critical cooling rate. Under the conventional definition, improved glass-forming ability corresponds to a lower critical cooling rate.
